Gluttonous
glŭt'ən-əs
adj. (given to excess in eating; the charge falsely laid against the Son of man)
Latin gluttire, to swallow or gulp down. The Greek phagos is simply an eater, used as an insult: a man defined by his appetite.

Biblical Definition

The word enters the New Testament as a slander against Christ. “The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children” (Mat 11:19); Luke records it in the same terms (Luk 7:34). The context is the Lord's complaint that His generation could not be pleased: John came neither eating nor drinking and they said he had a devil; the Son of man came eating and drinking and they called Him a glutton. The charge tells us nothing about Christ and everything about men who had already decided. Yet the sin itself is real and Scripture is severe about it. “For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Pro 23:21). Under the law a son past correction was charged in these very words before the elders: “This our son is stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton, and a drunkard” (Deu 21:20). The Bible is not squeamish about eating — it gives feasts, and it gives a Supper — but it knows the difference between a table received with thanksgiving and a belly made a god.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines gluttonous as given to excessive eating; greedy of eating; insatiable; and a glutton as one who indulges to excess in eating.

expand to see more

GLUTTON, n. [L. gluto, from glutio, to swallow.] One who indulges to excess in eating.

2. One eager of anything to excess.

GLUTTONOUS, a. Given to excessive eating; greedy of eating; insatiable.

Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber. Matt. xi.

Key Scripture

Mat 11:19 — "The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children."

Luk 7:34 — "The Son of man is come eating and drinking; and ye say, Behold a gluttonous man, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners!"

Pro 23:21 — "For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags."

Deu 21:20 — "And they shall say unto the elders of his city, This our son is stubborn and rebellious, he will not obey our voice; he is a glutton, and a drunkard."

Modern Corruption

The one sin of appetite the modern church will not name is the one the law named first, while the charge Christ actually bore — friend of publicans and sinners — is worn as a license.

expand to see more

Gluttony has quietly left the pulpit's list. Drunkenness is still preached against; excess at the table is treated as a matter of health, taste, or metabolism, and any mention of it is felt to be unkind. Two errors meet here and both must be refused. The first is the silence itself, which leaves a real work of the flesh unnamed — Paul writes of men whose god is their belly, and Proverbs joins the glutton to the drunkard in one sentence of consequence. The second error is the opposite overcorrection, in which weight becomes the measure of holiness and the thin man is assumed to be temperate. Scripture's category is not the shape of the body but the rule of the appetite: whether a man eats to the glory of God with thanksgiving, or is governed by what he wants. Fasting has all but disappeared from ordinary practice, and its disappearance is the plainest evidence that the appetite is not being examined at all.

The other corruption runs from the slander itself. Because our Lord was called a glutton and a winebibber for eating with publicans and sinners, some argue that any charge of excess against a Christian is proof of the accuser's pharisaism, and that being disreputable is itself a mark of gospel faithfulness. The text will not carry it. Christ ate with sinners and never sinned at their tables; He was falsely accused, which is a different thing from being rightly accused and dismissing it. His own answer is the standard: wisdom is justified of her children — the vindication comes from what the life produces, not from the accusation being loud. A man whose conduct is genuinely temperate may be slandered and should bear it. A man whose appetite genuinely rules him may not hide behind the slander that was laid on his Master.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek phagos (G5314), an eater, a glutton; Hebrew zalal (H2151), to be loose or worthless, used of the glutton; both set against egkrateia (G1466), temperance.

expand to see more

Greek phagos (G5314) — a glutton, literally an eater; used only in the slander against Christ; Matthew 11:19, Luke 7:34.

Hebrew zalal (H2151) — to shake out, to be loose, hence to squander or be a glutton; Deuteronomy 21:20, Proverbs 23:21.

Greek koilia (G2836) — the belly; whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame; Philippians 3:19.

Greek egkrateia (G1466) — temperance, self-mastery; the fruit of the Spirit that governs appetite; Galatians 5:23.

Greek oinopotes (G3630) — a winebibber, the companion charge in the same slander; Matthew 11:19.

Usage

"“Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber” — the slander a generation laid on Christ."

"“The drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty” — appetite and its wages."

"“Wisdom is justified of her children” — the vindication that comes from fruit, not from volume."
